lead: Multimedia presentations run several timed streams together: a video call has voice and lips, a class recording has slides and narration, a film has dialogue and subtitles. Synchronization keeps these media at the intended relative times during capture, transmission and presentation. Without it, lips move after the voice, slides jump ahead of the teacher, and subtitles spoil the next line. Players, editors, video-conferencing apps and e-learning systems use it every time they align a soundtrack to a picture.
prereq: You need: media types for samples and frames, and audio and video streams in containers.

blocks.text: Intra-stream synchronization keeps one stream's units evenly spaced. Video at 25 frames per second needs a frame every 1/25 s = 40 ms. Audio at 8 kHz needs a sample every 1/8000 s = 0.125 ms. If units arrive in a burst, the stream is wrong even when every unit is present.

Inter-stream synchronization keeps relative timing between streams, such as voice and lips. A synchronization point is a pair of timestamps that should align, such as one video frame and one audio block.

Delay is the time from capture to presentation. Jitter is the variation in delay: one packet takes 20 ms, the next 70 ms. Buffering holds data briefly so late packets play smoothly; it adds delay and cuts jitter. Skew is the remaining time difference between matching points after buffering. The goal is stable relative time, not zero delay. A player can hide small jitter with a buffer. The buffer can reorder units that arrive out of order but before their deadline; it cannot fix a unit that arrives after its deadline or is lost.

blocks.where: t<sub>audio</sub> is the audio presentation timestamp in ms; t<sub>video</sub> is the video presentation timestamp in ms; positive skew means audio is later than video.

blocks.text: Test sync with |skew| ≤ S, where S is the allowed skew in ms. A presentation interval is the window [t − S, t + S] in which a unit may be shown without breaking sync.

items: Find its matching unit in the other stream.
Compute skew and compare |skew| with S.
If audio is later by more than S, delay video by the skew when a buffer exists.

If audio is later, delay video; with no buffer, drop audio samples or repeat/freeze one video frame. If audio is earlier, delay audio; with no buffer, drop or duplicate video frames or audio samples under policy.

blocks.text: Buffering reduces jitter, not a permanent skew. Lip sync is the main test: the sound of a syllable and the mouth shape must fall in the same interval. Speech uses a tighter S than a slide show.

figure.caption: The video frame at 120 ms may pair with audio anywhere from 40 to 200 ms. Audio at 150 ms is 30 ms off, inside the window; audio at 230 ms is 110 ms off, outside it, so the player delays the video by 110 ms.

examples.question: A video frame has timestamp 120 ms and its matching audio sample has timestamp 150 ms. The allowed skew is S = 80 ms. (a) Find the skew and decide if they are in sync. (b) Repeat for audio timestamp 230 ms and state the player action.
steps: |skew| = 30 ms ≤ 80 ms, so the pair is in sync.
|skew| = 110 ms > 80 ms, so they are out of sync; audio is later.
Delay video by 110 ms if a buffer exists; otherwise drop audio samples to move audio earlier, or repeat/freeze one video frame to delay the picture. Do not skip video frames when audio is late.
examples.answer: Skew is +30 ms, inside the ±80 ms limit; for 230 ms the skew is +110 ms, so delay video by 110 ms if a buffer exists; otherwise drop audio samples or repeat/freeze one video frame.
examples.check:
def skew(tv, ta):
    return ta - tv
s1 = skew(120, 150)
s2 = skew(120, 230)
print(s1)
print(s2)

traps: Use |skew| against S; a negative skew can still be inside the limit.
Positive skew means audio is later than video, not earlier.
Buffering cuts jitter; it does not remove a fixed offset.
Convert frame rate to period: 25 fps is 40 ms per frame, not 25 ms.

quiz.a: It keeps the relative timing between two or more streams, such as audio and video.

quiz.q: What does a positive skew mean?
quiz.a: Audio is later than video at the matching point.

quiz.q: Why does buffering reduce jitter but not a permanent skew?
quiz.a: It absorbs delay variation, but a constant offset stays unless the scheduler adds or removes time.

quiz.q: Video timestamp 200 ms, audio 240 ms, S = 80 ms. Find skew and sync.
Video 500 ms, audio 640 ms, S = 80 ms. Find skew and action.
quiz.a: skew = 640 − 500 = +140 ms; 140 > 80, so delay video by 140 ms.

quiz.q: A player adds a 200 ms buffer. What happens to jitter and lip sync?
quiz.a: Jitter falls because late units wait; delay rises by 200 ms and a fixed skew remains, so lip sync can still fail.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry players use adaptive jitter buffers that grow when the network is unstable and shrink when it settles. Video-conferencing and live streaming use lip-sync correction with timestamp pairs; VR and AR add spatial audio alignment. Search next for 'inter-stream synchronization', 'jitter buffer' and 'lip sync correction'.
